notes: Ruling slot 13 = Republican Council of Abdul Rahman al-Iryani. MD's later bodies (GPC 1982, YSP 1978, Party of Truth and Islah 1990, Ansar Allah, AQAP) replaced by their 1970 predecessors/milieus: Saudi Special Committee clients (0), PDU and RDP (4/19), Union of Popular Forces (8), Saada Zaydi ulama (9), Muslim Brotherhood (12). NUPO kept in 14 and the two Ba'ath wings in 7/21 per MD. MD's League of Yemen's Sons (= South Arabian League) is a southern exile body and is placed in SYE slot 1 instead; Bakil takes slot 20. People's Socialist Party of the southern exiles in Taizz in 18.

0.name: Rijal al-Lajna al-Khassa
0.text:
The network of shaikhs, officers and officials on the payroll of Saudi Arabia's Special Committee for Yemeni affairs, chaired by Defence Minister Prince Sultan bin Abdulaziz. Built up during the civil war to fund the royalists, the committee has steadily shifted its stipends to republican tribal leaders as Riyadh moves towards accepting the republic.

Its men want a conservative, anti-communist Yemen Arab Republic under Saudi tutelage: royalists readmitted, leftists purged, the army kept weak and the tribes strong, and close ties with Washington and the Gulf monarchies. Their leverage is money: Saudi subsidies that buy loyalty across the north and can make or break a government in Sana'a.

1.name: Hashid
1.text:
The most powerful tribal confederation of the northern highlands, headed by its paramount shaikh Abdullah bin Husayn al-Ahmar, whose father and brother were executed by Imam Ahmad and who threw Hashid behind the republic in 1962. Al-Ahmar is one of the arbiters of the emerging post-war settlement and the leading voice of conservative republicanism.

Hashid stands for a republic rooted in Islam and tribal custom, with a consultative assembly of shaikhs and notables, reconciliation with Saudi Arabia and no truck with Marxists or Egyptian-style socialism. Pro-Saudi and therefore Western-leaning, its leverage lies in tens of thousands of armed tribesmen and the shaikh's role as kingmaker.

2.name: Al-Ahrar al-Yamaniyyun
2.text:
The constitutional reform movement founded in Aden in 1944 by Ahmad Muhammad Nu'man and the poet Muhammad Mahmud al-Zubayri, whose members joined the failed constitutional revolt of 1948 and the revolution of 1962. Zubayri was assassinated in 1965, but its veterans, Nu'man foremost among them, form the backbone of the civilian republican establishment.

The Ahrar stand for a constitutional, civilian republic: a written constitution, an elected consultative council, the rule of law, mass education and an end to both imamic despotism and military or foreign tutelage. Moderate and pragmatic, open to Western and Saudi aid, they are strongest among Taizz merchants, teachers, journalists and emigrants.

3.name: Ummal al-Hudayda
3.text:
The dockers of Hodeida's Soviet-built port, the workers of the Chinese-built textile mill in Sana'a and the drivers, mechanics and builders of the republic's growing towns, many of them returnees from Aden's unions after 1967. Small unions and workers' committees have formed in Hodeida, Taizz and Sana'a, tolerated but closely watched by the government.

They seek legal trade unions, a labour code, wage rises, social insurance and housing, pursued through bargaining and reform rather than revolution. Moderate and practical, open to Western and Arab aid as much as to Eastern, their leverage lies in their ability to halt the port and the few factories on which the state's revenue depends.

4.name: Ittihad al-Sha'b al-Dimuqrati
4.text:
Yemen's oldest Marxist-Leninist party, founded in Aden in 1961 by Abdullah Abd al-Razzaq Badhib as an organisation for the whole of Yemen. While Badhib and its southern leaders now cooperate with the ruling National Front in Aden, its northern cells are illegal and work secretly among students, teachers and workers in Taizz, Hodeida and Sana'a.

It holds that both Yemens must pass through a national-democratic revolution to socialism under a vanguard party, and looks to the Soviet Union as model and patron. Small but disciplined, it supplies the northern left with theory and cadres; its leverage lies in its links to Aden and Moscow.

5.name: Al-Muqawama al-Sha'biyya
5.text:
The armed militias of workers, students and townsmen raised in Sana'a during the seventy-day royalist siege of 1967-1968, when the Egyptian army had withdrawn and the capital's left defended it street by street. After the siege the government disarmed and disbanded them, and the clashes of August 1968 broke their leftist officer allies.

Their survivors, now underground or in Aden, hold that the revolution of 1962 has been betrayed by shaikhs and Saudi money, and call for armed struggle, land to the peasants and unity with the revolutionary South. Radical and impatient, their leverage lies in hidden arms, the Shafi'i lower provinces and the support of Aden's National Front.

6.name: Ansar al-Sallal
6.text:
The die-hard loyalists of Abdullah al-Sallal, the officer who proclaimed the republic in September 1962 and ruled under Egyptian protection until he was deposed while abroad in November 1967; he now lives in exile in Iraq. His following survives among officers, officials and veterans of the Egyptian years who regard the present leadership's course as surrender.

They oppose any compromise with the royalists or Saudi Arabia, demand the army's primacy in politics and look to Cairo, Baghdad and Moscow for weapons and backing. Authoritarian and anti-Western, they lack a mass base but keep connections in the officer corps and among republicans who fought through the whole civil war.

7.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki
7.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki - Qutr al-Yaman
7.text:
The Yemeni branch of the Ba'ath, organised since the late 1950s among officers, teachers and students, especially in Taizz and the lower provinces. Since the 1966 split in the party, the faction loyal to the military Ba'athists of Damascus and Salah Jadid's leadership works clandestinely in the army and the schools of the Yemen Arab Republic.

It seeks a socialist, unitary Arab republic run by the party and the army, land reform, state industry and close ties with Syria and the Soviet Union, and condemns the Sana'a leadership's turn towards Riyadh. Anti-Western and authoritarian, its leverage lies in cells within the officer corps and the ministries.

8.name: Ittihad al-Quwa al-Sha'biyya
8.text:
A Zaydi reformist movement founded in the early 1960s by Ibrahim bin Ali al-Wazir, scion of the family of sayyids that led the constitutional revolt of 1948. Rejecting both the Hamid al-Din imams and the Egyptian-backed military republic, it joined the Third Force of the mid-1960s that pressed for a negotiated peace between royalists and republicans.

It calls for a shura-based Islamic state that preserves Zaydi learning and the role of the sayyids within a constitutional order, with elected councils and accountable rulers. Neutral between the blocs and close to the reconciliation now taking shape, its leverage lies in its prestige among Zaydi scholars, sayyid families and northern notables.

9.name: Ulama Sa'da
9.text:
The Zaydi scholars of Saada and the far north, heartland of the imamate and the royalist cause, among them Majd al-Din al-Mu'ayyadi and Badr al-Din al-Huthi. For them the imamate is not merely a dynasty but a religious duty: the community must be led by a learned descendant of the Prophet who rises against injustice.

They regard the republic as an assault on Zaydism by Shafi'i officers and Egyptian secularists, and refuse any settlement that abandons the imamate as an institution. Hostile to both superpowers, they command deep loyalty among the tribes of Saada and Khawlan; their leverage lies in sermons, religious schools and the doctrine of armed revolt.

10.name: Ulama Zabid
10.text:
The Shafi'i ulama of Zabid, Bayt al-Faqih and the Tihama, heirs of one of the oldest centres of Sunni learning in Arabia, together with the muftis and qadis of the lower highlands. Long subordinate under the Zaydi imams, most welcomed the republic that ended Zaydi rule and now serve as judges, teachers and preachers of the new state.

They stand for orthodox Sunni law, obedience to legitimate authority, religious education and close ties with Saudi Arabia and the conservative monarchies, while rejecting Marxism and secular nationalism. Quietist and establishment-minded, their leverage lies in the mosques and courts of the Tihama and the populous Shafi'i south.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
The Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, outlawed in every Arab state and organised in secret cells. In Yemen it has won a handful of followers among students returning from Jordan, Kuwait and Iraq and among teachers in Sana'a and Taizz.

It condemns the republic, the imamate and the Marxist left alike as un-Islamic and calls for the restoration of the caliphate across the Muslim world, to be won by persuading army officers and notables to hand it power. Rejecting both superpowers and every existing government, it has no armed wing; its leverage lies in disciplined, patient recruitment.

12.name: Jama'at al-Ikhwan al-Muslimin
12.text:
The Yemeni branch of the movement founded in Egypt by Hassan al-Banna, whose emissary al-Fudayl al-Wartilani helped plan the constitutional revolt of 1948. Its members, among them Abdu Muhammad al-Mikhlafi and the preacher Abd al-Majid al-Zindani, organise among students, teachers and officers and have won influence in education.

It seeks an Islamic republic grounded in sharia, the spread of religious schools and the defeat of Marxist and Nasserist secularism, while working within the republican establishment alongside conservative shaikhs. Anti-communist and close to Saudi and Kuwaiti patrons, its leverage lies in the classroom, the mosque and its alliance with tribal conservatives.

13.name: Al-Majlis al-Jumhuri
13.text:
The collective presidency that has ruled the Yemen Arab Republic since the bloodless coup of 5 November 1967 removed Abdullah al-Sallal. Its chairman, Qadi Abdul Rahman al-Iryani, a civilian jurist and veteran of the 1948 revolt, presides over a balance of shaikhs, officers and politicians, with Abdullah al-Kurshumi as prime minister.

The Council seeks to end the civil war on republican terms: royalists readmitted to state posts but the Hamid al-Din family excluded, a permanent constitution and consultative council, and reconciliation with Saudi Arabia. Non-aligned, accepting Soviet arms and Western and Saudi money alike, its authority depends on al-Iryani's prestige and the goodwill of the great tribes and the army.

14.name: Al-Tanzim al-Wahdawi al-Sha'bi al-Nasiri
14.text:
A clandestine network of Yemeni admirers of Gamal Abdel Nasser, organised in the mid-1960s among officers, students and officials who served alongside the Egyptian expeditionary force. Since the Egyptian withdrawal of 1967 and Sallal's fall, the Nasserists have lost their patron in Sana'a and operate secretly, especially in Taizz and the army.

They stand for Arab unity, the union of the two Yemens, a strong developmental state, land reform and positive neutralism between the blocs, rejecting both Marxist class struggle and Saudi tutelage. Their leverage lies in officers trained in Egypt and the enduring popularity of Nasser among the urban young.

15.name: Sharikat Ha'il Sa'id An'am
15.text:
The trading house founded in Aden in 1938 by Hayel Saeed Anam, a self-made merchant from al-Hujariyya south of Taizz, which grew rich on the import, distribution and processing trades of the British colony. With the National Front's nationalisations in the South, the family is shifting its operations to Taizz and Hodeida, where it is becoming the republic's leading industrial group.

It wants stability, open trade, low taxes, cheap credit and state protection for infant industry, and prefers a quiet government in Sana'a that keeps the leftists at bay. Pragmatic and well connected in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf, its leverage lies in capital, jobs and the patronage it extends across the Shafi'i south.

16.name: Tujjar al-Mahjar
16.text:
The traders and remittance agents of the Yemeni diaspora, from the souks of Jeddah and Riyadh and the ports of East Africa and Ethiopia to the Yemeni communities of Britain and Detroit, whose money now keeps much of the republic afloat. Many are returning to invest in shops, transport and building in Sana'a, Taizz and Ibb.

They want free movement of money and people, low customs, private enterprise and a light-handed state that guarantees property and contracts, and fear both Marxist confiscations and tribal extortion. Indifferent to the blocs, their leverage lies in hard currency: no government can pay its bills without the emigrant economy.

17.name: Hurras al-Mudarrajat
17.text:
The highland villagers, terrace builders and water elders of the mountains between Ibb, Taizz and Sana'a, whose stone terraces, cisterns and spring channels have sustained farming for millennia. War, the emigration of young men and the spread of qat in place of coffee and grain are leaving terraces to collapse and soils to wash away.

They call for the repair of terraces and cisterns, protection of springs and woodland, support for coffee and grain over qat, and respect for customary water law. Rooted in village councils and religious endowments, distant from the blocs, their leverage lies in the peasantry that still makes up most of the population.

18.name: Hizb al-Sha'b al-Ishtiraki
18.text:
The labour party founded in Aden in 1962 by Abdullah al-Asnaj as the political arm of the Aden Trade Union Congress. Defeated by the National Front in the struggle for southern independence, al-Asnaj and thousands of his followers now live in the Yemen Arab Republic, chiefly in Taizz, where the party acts as a bridge between the southern exiles and the northern republic.

It stands for democratic Arab socialism: free trade unions, a planned but plural economy, Yemeni unity and close ties with Nasser's Egypt, opposing both Aden's Marxism and Saudi conservatism. Its leverage lies in organised workers, southern exiles and al-Asnaj's standing in Cairo and Sana'a.

19.name: Al-Hizb al-Dimuqrati al-Thawri al-Yamani
19.text:
The Marxist party formed in 1968 by the northern branch of the Arab Nationalist Movement, which turned from Nasserism to scientific socialism after the defeat of 1967. Its leading theorist is Sultan Ahmad Umar, and its cadres, purged from the army and administration after the clashes of August 1968, organise underground in Taizz, Ibb and the Hujariyya.

It calls for a national-democratic revolution: land reform, the destruction of tribal and feudal power, mass organisations and unification with the South under a revolutionary vanguard. Close to Aden's National Front left but jealous of its independence, it looks to no single foreign capital; its leverage lies in the peasants and students of the Shafi'i midlands.

20.name: Bakil
20.text:
The largest tribal confederation of Yemen, spread across the plateau north and east of Sana'a and divided during the civil war between republican sections, such as Nihm under Shaikh Sinan Abu Luhum, and royalist sections in the east. As the war ends, its shaikhs are bargaining hard for their place in the new order.

Bakil's politics are those of tribal populism: shares for every tribe in the army, budget and posts, resentment of Hashid's predominance, distrust of townsmen, foreigners and parties, and the defence of tribal law against the central state. Courted by Riyadh and Sana'a alike, its leverage lies in numbers, arms and the ability to cut the roads around the capital.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki - al-Qiyada al-Qawmiyya
21.english: Arab Socialist Ba'ath Party - Yemen Region (pro-Iraqi)
21.native_full: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki - al-Qiyada al-Qawmiyya
21.text:
The Ba'athists who sided with Michel Aflaq's National Command in the 1966 split and look to the regime installed in Baghdad in July 1968. Organised in secret cells among officers, students and teachers, and in tribal families whose sons studied in Iraq, it is the faction that Baghdad now cultivates most generously in Yemen.

It preaches pan-Arab nationalism of the hardest kind: one Arab nation, a disciplined party-state, a militarised society and implacable hostility to imperialism, Zionism and Persian influence. Funded and armed by Baghdad, its leverage lies in Iraqi money, scholarships and the officers it has placed in the army.

22.name: Al-Quwwat al-Musallaha al-Yamaniyya
22.text:
The republican army, built since 1962 with Egyptian instructors and Soviet weapons, and rebuilt after the Egyptian withdrawal of 1967 around the units that held Sana'a during the royalist siege. Under General Hassan al-Amri, who crushed the leftist officers in August 1968, it has become a largely Zaydi-officered force allied with the great tribes.

The army sees itself as guardian of the republic against royalists and Marxists alike, and its commanders expect a decisive voice in government and a share of Saudi and Soviet aid. Still small, poorly paid and dependent on tribal levies, its leverage lies in control of the capital and the main roads.

23.name: Bayt Hamid al-Din
23.text:
The Zaydi dynasty that ruled the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen from 1918 until the revolution of September 1962. Imam Muhammad al-Badr, deposed a week after succeeding his father, led the royalist war from the northern mountains with Saudi help, while his cousin Prince Muhammad bin al-Husayn has directed much of the royalist effort in recent years.

The royalists seek the restoration of the imamate as an Islamic monarchy under Zaydi law. But Saudi aid is drying up, many royalist shaikhs are making their peace with Sana'a and the family faces exclusion from any settlement; its leverage now lies in residual loyalty among northern Zaydi tribes and in its Saudi hosts.
